prompt: Why must radical chlorination of methane use EXCESS methane (CH₄ in large excess, Cl₂ limiting)?

options.label: Each product (CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃) still has C-H bonds Cl• can abstract — excess CH₄ makes Cl• hit UNreacted methane statistically
The reaction is highly exothermic — excess CH₄ absorbs heat as thermal ballast to prevent runaway
Radical chains terminate quickly without a large concentration of substrate to keep propagation going
Methane acts as the solvent — Cl₂ needs a nonpolar medium to dissociate photochemically into Cl•

explanation: The problem is POLYhalogenation: once CH₃Cl forms, it still has 3 C-H bonds that Cl• can abstract, giving CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, CCl₄. With excess CH₄, probability favors hitting unreacted CH₄, maximizing mono-chlorination yield. Industrial production of CHCl₃ or CCl₄ deliberately uses the opposite ratio to drive over-chlorination.
